titre_video: World War 3 Protocol. Why Global Nuclear Annihilation Is Inevitable.

segments.titre: The 6-minute countdown begins: a 3:04 a.m. nuclear alert
segments.resume: Opening hook: the world is minutes from annihilation and the "red button" on the president's desk is a myth, because the real system is a ticking clock. In a scenario at T-minus 6 minutes, 3:04 a.m., a Pentagon call wakes the president with news of incoming nuclear missiles and only 360 seconds to decide.
segments.texte: Right now, the world is just minutes away from total annihilation. The red button on the president's desk is a lie. The real system is a ticking clock, and it's already running down. When humanity is standing on the brink of total destruction, one person must make a decision that will vaporize hundreds of millions of people, and they only have 360 seconds to choose. T-minus 6 minutes, 3:04 a.m. A phone screams in the executive residence. A breathless voice from the Pentagon is on the other end. It is the nightmare scenario no president wants to hear. Incoming nuclear missiles have been detected. The countdown is live.

segments.titre: The football: the 45-lb presidential emergency satchel
segments.resume: No red button exists: a rotating military aide carries a 45-lb black leather briefcase, the presidential emergency satchel nicknamed the football after the early war plan Dropkick. It has followed every president for over 60 years, built from laminated cards and encrypted radio signals to eliminate hesitation.
segments.texte: The first thing the president doesn't do is reach for the nuclear button. That doesn't exist. Instead, a military officer bursts into the room carrying a 45-lb black leather briefcase. >> [music] >> The aid carrying it is a rotating officer from one of the five service branches. They shadow the commander-in-chief constantly. They're never more than a few steps away, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, every single day of a presidency. That briefcase has followed every American president for more than 60 years. It rides in the same motorcade. It boards the same plane, waits outside the same rooms. It [music] is always within reach. The official name is the presidential emergency satchel. >> [music] >> Everyone who works around it calls it the football. This name traces back to an early nuclear war plan with the code name dropkick, football being the obvious shorthand. Inside is a bureaucratic machine assembled across six decades, built out of laminated cards and encrypted radio signals. It's designed to [music] do one thing: eliminate hesitation. And hesitate is the one thing that the president can't do right now.

segments.titre: What the football does: identity, communications and the nuclear menu
segments.resume: The football locks in the president's identity to the National Military Command Center, provides secure communications and holds a simplified menu of strike options. Garrett Graff and Colonel Buzz Patterson compared it to a Denny's menu or ordering at a Chinese restaurant. All it takes to authorize a launch is a credit-card-sized piece of plastic.
segments.texte: T-minus 5 minutes, 30 seconds. The officer slams the briefcase down on a desk and rips open the zippers. As the seconds tick away, the president fights the grogginess and prepares for the most important decision in human history. The football does three things. First, it locks in the president's identity to the National Military Command Center at the Pentagon. Second, it provides secure communications to initiate a launch order. And third, it contains a simplified menu of nuclear strike options. Journalist Garrett Graff, who wrote a definitive account of the football for CNN, reported that aides have described a laminated visual guide inside the briefcase as looking like a Denny's menu of nuclear war. Military aide and Air Force Colonel Buzz Patterson, who carried the football for President Clinton, described the selection process as picking one menu option out of column A and two out of column B, like ordering at a Chinese restaurant. Each option represents a different scale of nuclear destruction. Everything from a limited strike to something that eliminates entire regions of the planet. There is no retina scanner inside of the football. There is no red button. All it takes is a single piece of plastic roughly the size of a credit card, and that card has the potential to be the most dangerous object in the world. Without it, America is about to be a radioactive wasteland.

segments.titre: The missing biscuit: the president cannot find the gold codes
segments.resume: In the scenario the president scrambles for the laminated authentication card known as the biscuit or gold codes and finds only empty wood. Without reading the codes on the card the Pentagon will refuse to fire, and cold sweat breaks as the president realizes this is no drill.
segments.texte: T-minus 5 minutes. The president throws back the bedsheets, scrambles blindly for [music] the small laminated card known as the biscuit or the gold codes. Whatever its name, it's not [music] there. All the president finds is empty wood. To authorize the end of the world, the president has to read the codes printed on the card. Without them, the Pentagon will refuse to fire. Cold sweat breaks across his forehead. This isn't a drill. It's history repeating itself.

segments.titre: Real biscuit mishaps: Carter's dry cleaner and Reagan's shooting
segments.resume: Jimmy Carter, a former nuclear submarine engineer, simplified the nuclear protocol, creating the biscuit, then left it in a suit pocket sent to the dry cleaner. After John Hinckley shot Reagan in March 1981, the biscuit was left in a shoe at George Washington University Hospital and the FBI returned it two days later.
segments.texte: Decades earlier, Jimmy Carter, a former nuclear submarine engineer, demanded the nuclear protocol be simplified. The original process was too slow, too wieldy to survive a nuclear attack. So, the biscuit was born. And then, Carter put it into a suit pocket and sent it to the dry cleaner. While a hypothetical nuclear countdown was ticking, the literal key to the nuclear arsenal was spinning around a washing machine. Ronald Reagan's situation was infinitely darker. In March 1981, John Hinckley shot Reagan outside the Washington Hilton Hotel. As doctors frantically cut the president's clothes off in the emergency room, no one thought to secure the biscuit. It was eventually tucked into one of Reagan's shoes in the trauma bay in George Washington University Hospital. The FBI eventually found it and returned it to the White House two days later.

segments.titre: Finding the codes and rushing to the bunker
segments.resume: At T-minus 4 minutes 30 seconds the president finds the biscuit in a suit jacket pocket and reads the authentication codes, but the phone to the Pentagon only gives static. Secret Service agents rush the president through a corridor and elevator into a reinforced bunker with the football as the blast doors slam shut.
segments.texte: None of that matters to the current president. All All knows is that America is on the verge of being wiped out and the clock is ticking. T-minus 4 minutes 30 seconds. The president springs from the bed and rummages through drawers, aids up in furniture. Then the president's fingers feel cold hard plastic buried in a pocket of a suit jacket, the biscuit. He pulls it out, cracks the plastic [music] and stares at the authentication codes. An aid holds a phone. He's met with static. The Pentagon is out of reach. Just then Secret Service agents burst into the presidential bedroom. They grab the president and barrel him down a corridor into an elevator and through reinforced doors. The football follows him. The heavy blast doors slam shut sealing them all inside with a metallic thud.

segments.titre: ICBM vs SLBM flight times and the 3.5-minute window
segments.resume: An ICBM from Russia takes roughly 26 to 30 minutes to arrive and is detected immediately by satellites thanks to its heat signature. Submarine-launched missiles can be fired from hundreds of miles off the coast in about 15 minutes or even 10. A 1982 Joint Chiefs study found about 3.5 minutes between a missile breaking the surface and strikes on command centers.
segments.texte: When an intercontinental ballistic missile launches from Russian soil, it takes roughly 26 to 30 minutes to reach the continental United States. That buys them time to think and verify and consult, but ICBM launches are detectable from the moment of launch thanks to their enormous heat signatures. They're picked up immediately from surveillance satellites, but submarine launched ballistic missiles? They're different. An enemy submarine can position itself hundreds of miles off the American coastline without detection. A missile launched from that position has more like [music] 15 minutes of travel time. If the submarine is positioned close enough, the window of detection and impact collapses to somewhere closer to 10. But a 1982 Joint Chiefs of Staff historical study exposed an even more brutal reality. In certain SLBM scenarios, there can be about 3 and 1/2 minutes between the moment a missile breaks the surface and direct strikes on the nation's command centers. The entire command structure can be obliterated before it has a chance to decide how to respond, which means by the time the president reads his identification codes, the room he is standing in might already be gone.

segments.titre: Early warning chain: NORAD, STRATCOM and confidence levels
segments.resume: Missile tracking data flows at the speed of light to NORAD in Colorado, US Strategic Command in Nebraska and the National Military Command Center. Analysts calculate the trajectory and assign a low, medium or high confidence level, which is why the president was woken at 3:04 a.m. The STRATCOM commander briefs the president on the threat, response options and civilian casualties.
segments.texte: T-minus 4 minutes. The atmosphere crackles. The president and his aids frantically try to reconnect with the Pentagon. As the missiles move closer, information travels at the speed of light to early warning teams at NORAD in Colorado, US Strategic Command in Nebraska, and the National Military Command Center at the Pentagon. Analysts pull up the tracking data. They calculate the trajectory and assign a confidence level, low, medium, or high. That was why the president was woken up at 3:04 a.m. The STRATCOM commander briefs the president on the threat, the available response options, and what each option means in terms of civilian casualties on both sides.

segments.titre: 1995 Norwegian rocket incident: Yeltsin activates the Cheget
segments.resume: In January 1995 Russian early-warning radar detected a rocket off Norway resembling a US Trident missile. It was actually a Black Brant XII research rocket launched to study the aurora, notified to 30 countries but never passed on to radar technicians. Boris Yeltsin's Cheget was activated for the first time in an emergency, and after eight minutes the rocket curved out to sea and the alert was stood down.
segments.texte: President's mind races. Could it be a mistake? That's happened before. Back in January 1995, Russian scientists at an early warning radar station in the northwestern part of the country detected an unidentified rocket rising somewhere off the Norwegian coast. The radar track showed a missile ascending on a trajectory that was nearly identical to a US Trident submarine missile, the kind that could be used to blind Russian radar and command systems before a larger first strike. Russian military protocols activated immediately. But what the radar operators did not know was that Norwegian and American scientists had just launched a four-stage Black Brant 12 research rocket to study the aurora borealis. They had notified 30 countries in advance, including Russia. The Russian Foreign Ministry received the notification. The information never made it to the radar technicians. An anonymous Russian general later explained that officials have taken a literal attitude toward the notice, assuming it was meant for sailors, not military personnel. For the next 8 minutes, Russian radar tracked the rocket. Protocol required a decision be made before the decision window closed. A real Trident from the Barents Sea would reach mainland Russia in approximately 10 minutes. Russian submarine commanders were ordered into combat readiness. Boris Yeltsin, the president of Russia, was notified and his Cheget, the Russian nuclear briefcase equivalent, was activated. It was the first and only time in recorded history that a Russian president's nuclear briefcase had ever been turned on [music] in a genuine emergency. Yeltsin had to decide whether to initiate a retaliatory nuclear strike against the United States. At minute 8, Russian observers determined the rocket was curving away from Russian territory. It was headed toward the open sea. The alert was stood down.

segments.titre: Attack verified; Bruce Blair on the 6-minute decision flaw
segments.resume: At T-minus 3 minutes 30 seconds ground radar confirms the missiles in mid-flight, so a second independent system verifies the attack. Former Minuteman launch officer Bruce Blair explains the president has roughly 6 minutes to decide in a rushed, mechanical process, and warns of the flaw of an irrational, panicked or incapacitated president.
segments.texte: This time the president might not be so lucky. T-minus 3 minutes 30 seconds. Ground-based radar systems confirmed the missiles are in mid- flight. The attack is now verified by a second independent system. This situation is terrifyingly real. Nuclear security expert and former Minuteman ICBM launch officer Bruce Blair, a man who spent a career studying the system from the inside, put it directly. The president has roughly 6 minutes to make a decision if it appears we are under attack. He added that the whole process is very rushed and very mechanical. That's just the physics of nuclear retaliation. But Blair also exposed a huge flaw, one that was swept under the rug during the Cold War. What if the president acts irrationally or panic-stricken? Even worse, what if they're already incapacitated?

segments.titre: The Soviet Dead Hand (Perimeter) system
segments.resume: In 1985 the Soviet Union activated Perimeter, called Dead Hand in the West, to preserve mutually assured destruction against a decapitation strike. It monitors seismic activity, radiation, air pressure and heat and, if the command structure is incapacitated, launches a command rocket that broadcasts launch orders to all surviving nuclear forces. It is believed to remain operational today.
segments.texte: The Soviets already had an answer for that back in 1985. The Soviet Union quietly activated a system they called the Perimeter. In the West, it earned another nickname, the Dead Hand. It was built on an assumption of what might happen if American missiles destroyed Soviet leadership so completely and quickly that nobody survived to authorize retaliation. The entire political stability of mutually assured destruction or MAD depends on both sides being able to respond. If you could decapitate the Soviet command structure in a surprise first strike, MAD breaks down. The threat of retaliation disappears because there's nobody left to retaliate. Dead Hand was the answer to that problem. It's a system that monitors seismic activity, radiation levels, air pressure, and heat across the Russian territory. If those sensors pick up patterns consistent with nuclear detonations and the command structure is incapacitated, Dead Hand can autonomously launch a command rocket. That command rocket carries a radio transmitter rather than a warhead. It broadcasts launch orders to every surviving Russian nuclear asset on the ground, including silos, submarines, and mobile launchers. Even if every human in the Russian chain of command has been killed, the missiles launch. Perimeter became operational in 1985 and based on available evidence has remained operational into the present day. Whatever happens, the missiles are coming.

segments.titre: Launch on warning doctrine
segments.resume: As red lights strobe in the White House bunker and monitors track missile plumes, the narrator explains launch on warning: launching missiles upon detecting an attack before enemy warheads land. Fixed-silo ICBMs are vulnerable, so waiting to absorb a first strike could destroy the arsenal, which pushes states to launch early.
segments.texte: T minus 3 minutes. The clock is ticking. Red lights strobe across the secure White House bunker. Aids frantically scream into phones. Monitors track a cluster of red plumes arcing over the northern hemisphere. Humanity is trapped in a 6-minute nightmare, and most people don't even realize how we got here. The answer lies in a military doctrine most people have never even heard of called [music] launch on warning. It's simple in concept, but apocalyptic in execution. If you detect an incoming attack, you launch your missiles before the enemy's missiles land. The reasoning is straightforward. ICBMs in fixed silos are vulnerable to incoming warheads. If you wait to absorb a first strike before retaliating, your arsenal might already be destroyed. So, you launch early. You keep your weapons alive by getting them off the ground before the enemy's weapons arrive.

segments.titre: Sole presidential launch authority
segments.resume: The United States has no known Dead Hand system, so a nuclear launch depends solely on the commander-in-chief, a weight no one else carries. At T-minus 2 minutes the American war machine grinds forward and stopping nuclear war becomes almost impossible.
segments.texte: T-minus 2 minutes, 30 seconds. The United States does not have a dead hand system that we know of. A nuclear launch depends solely on the commander-in-chief. No one else has the authority to launch a strike on a rival nation. It's a weight that no other person can carry. T-minus 2 minutes. The American war machine grinds forward. Generals whisper prayers. The president clasps his hands. America is at nuclear war, and stopping it is almost impossible.

segments.titre: 1979 NORAD false alarm caused by a war game tape
segments.resume: In November 1979 NORAD early warning computers showed hundreds of Soviet missiles heading for the US, bombers were put on alert and threat conferences were convened for about six minutes. Backup radars showed empty skies: a technician had loaded a realistic war game simulation into the live operational computer, which could not distinguish it from reality.
segments.texte: In November 1979, the early warning computers at NORAD suddenly lit up. Russia had launched a nuclear strike. Hundreds of missiles were heading right for the US. >> [music] >> Threat assessment conferences were called immediately. Tactical bombers were on high alert, sitting on the tarmac of America's air bases. For 6 minutes, the US military was ready to respond before the president made his decision. Analysts checked the backup radars. The skies were empty. A technician had accidentally uploaded a realistic war game into the live operational computer. The system couldn't tell the difference between the simulation and real life.

segments.titre: The three-tier menu of nuclear strike options
segments.resume: At T-minus 1 minute the president authenticates with the biscuit codes and chooses from a three-tiered menu. Limited attack options use a few warheads on military targets but look like an opening strike, selected options hit regional military forces, and major attack options launch thousands of warheads, a 1971 list including some 6,500 targets, wiping out leadership and nuclear forces.
segments.texte: Unfortunately for the president, this is very much real. T-minus 1 minute. >> [music] >> The president stares at the football as he utters the biscuit codes down the line. His identity is confirmed. He has seconds to choose from a three-tiered menu of death. At the bottom are the limited attack options. A small number of warheads directed at specific military targets. The strategic logic is to hit something precise, demonstrate capability, and invite the other side to stop before the world burns. The fatal problem from the enemy's perspective, a few incoming warheads look like the opening wave of a larger strike, it only triggers the same 6-minute decision window on the opposite side. In the middle are the selected attack options, a broader strike against regional military forces, naval assets, and military infrastructure. This signals the intent to launch a war, not necessarily a nuclear one. At the top are the major attack options, launching thousands of warheads against thousands of targets simultaneously. In 1971, that list included some 6,500 decapitates the enemy leadership, command posts, and nuclear forces in one fell swoop. The entire infrastructure of a civilization methodically eliminated. He makes his selection and signs the death warrant for millions.

segments.titre: The emergency action message and launch: no latitude to question an order
segments.resume: At T-minus 30 seconds the president's voice becomes an emergency action message sent to submarines, silos and bomber crews. Two-person crews verify it and turn their launch keys, and Bruce Blair notes there is no latitude to question an order because the authentication chain is complete. At T-minus 0 the missiles launch and cannot be recalled, the football being only the trigger mechanism.
segments.texte: T-minus 30 seconds. This is the moment the president's voice becomes an emergency action message. The encrypted command is simultaneously sent to submarines, missile silos, and bomber crew pilots on standby across the planet. Two-person crews at missile silos and aboard submarines independently verify the message. They physically turn their launch keys in the weapons. They don't bother calling you back or asking for confirmation. As nuclear expert Bruce Blair said, "There's really no latitude to question an order. The authentication chain is already complete." T-minus 0 minutes, 0 seconds. The missiles roar out of the silos and into the air. What happens next is all down to physics and fate. The missiles are on their way. It's an order that can't be taken back. The 6-minute window worked perfectly. There's nothing to do but wait. The football is just the trigger mechanism.

segments.titre: Scenario: a Taiwan crisis escalates into nuclear use by China
segments.resume: The scenario switches to Xi Jinping rushed into a bunker as nukes head toward Chinese bases and cities. A naval standoff over Taiwan escalates through airspace violations, sunk vessels and downed satellites, and with its conventional options narrowing China chooses nuclear weapons to shock the system and force results rather than win the war.
segments.texte: Xi Jinping's worst nightmare has arrived as he's rushed into a secure bunker. Nukes are flying toward Chinese military bases and cities. Could China really defend its homeland against a nuclear attack? The crisis that was supposed to stay contained over Taiwan is now spiraling out of control. What began as a naval standoff years earlier quickly evolved into close calls, airspace violations, and misread signals. Soon the United States moves forces into the region to stabilize the situation. Stabilization is not exactly the word Beijing would use, and things get real very fast. Both sides insist they're acting defensively right up to the point where defensive actions start to lead to the sinking of naval vessels and knocking satellites out of the sky. Facing mounting losses and pressure to protect Taiwan, the US signals that it's willing to escalate. China sees its conventional options narrowing and its credibility is on the line and decides to play ball. Beijing can't bend to America's terms. Nuclear weapons aren't launched to win the war or even end it, but to shock the system, to force results.

segments.titre: Limited vs full-scale nuclear assault on China
segments.resume: There are two ways the nuclear scenario could unfold. In the first, a small number of strikes on bases, command centers and infrastructure aims at coercion rather than annihilation, the limited nuclear use policymakers cling to. In the second, a full-scale assault overwhelms defenses, interceptors run out and the question becomes how much of the country can keep functioning.
segments.texte: And there are two very different versions of how this nuclear scenario might unfold. In the first, nuclear weapons are used in [music] a small number of strikes and aimed at military bases, command centers, and key infrastructure. The goal isn't annihilation, but coercion, an attempt to change the direction of the war >> [music] >> without setting the entire world on fire. This is the scaled version of a doomsday scenario policymakers cling to when they talk about limited nuclear use, even though the residents of the city where [music] a tactical nuke detonates would obviously beg to differ. The second option is a lot more apocalyptic. Instead of a handful of incoming warheads, China faces a full-scale nuclear assault designed to overwhelm its defenses from every direction at once. Missile systems will still engage as warnings go out, but the math changes fast as interceptors run out and decisions come too quickly. At that point, the question really stops being how much damage can China prevent, but how much of the country can survive functioning at all.

segments.titre: China's early warning satellites and long-range radars
segments.resume: Defending against nuclear missiles requires seeing them coming, and China has built its own early warning network. Since 2010 it has developed infrared satellites, launched from 2017 as communications technology experiment satellites, plus huge radars spotting launches from almost 2,500 miles, including one trained on Alaska and others in Fujian and Xinjiang.
segments.texte: There's something crucial to understand about defending against nuclear missiles. You can have all the latest interceptors in the world, but if the defending country can't accurately see what's coming, they are basically playing dodgeball while blindfolded. China gets this. >> [music] >> Back in 2010, they began building their own version of America's early warning satellite network. >> [music] >> By 2017, they started launching what they innocuously called communications technology experiment satellites, systems that watch for the thermal signature of missile [music] launches. Their sole purpose is to spot the infrared bloom of an intercontinental ballistic missile or ICBM engine almost 22,000 mi below. And satellites are only part of the story. China has constructed some absolutely massive radar installation units that can spot a missile launch from almost 2,500 mi away. They've [music] been strategically placed across the country, including one trained on Alaska, because [music] that's where American ICBMs would come from. Other systems are located in Fujian and Xinjiang, covering other approaches.

segments.titre: China's layered missile defense: HQ-9C, HQ-19 and HQ-29
segments.resume: At its September 2025 parade China showed three anti-ballistic missile layers: the HQ-9C against low-altitude short and medium-range missiles, the HQ-19 with Type 610A radar comparable to THAAD, and the mobile exoatmospheric HQ-29 hitting missiles above 93 miles. On paper this makes a sophisticated golden dome, though paper and reality differ.
segments.texte: At their September 2025 military parade, China rolled out their latest defensive arsenal like a deadly parade at a dictator's trade show. There were three anti-ballistic missile systems on display, designed to work as layers of a shield, which will figure prominently in any Chinese nuclear scenario. The HQ-9C is the first layer, and it handles all the low-altitude grunt work. This is China's nuclear goalkeeper targeting the medium- and short-range missiles already screaming toward their targets. Then there's the HQ-19, designed to take out missiles at altitudes slightly higher, up to 125 mi and traveling at almost 33,000 ft per second. The HQ-19 is guided by the Type 610A radar, and is comparable to America's THAAD system. It can hit ballistic missiles in the 1,800 to 2,500 range class, and that covers most regional threats. The HQ-29 is [music] the crown jewel of the Chinese defense triad. It's an exoatmospheric interceptor that works outside of the atmosphere entirely, targeting missiles in their mid-course phase at altitudes exceeding 93 mi. And unlike America's ground-based interceptors that sit in fixed silos, the HQ-29 is mobile. Mounted on launcher vehicles, it can pop up wherever it's needed. In theory, it's all quite impressive. A layered defense combining early warning satellites, massive ground radar, and three tiers of interceptor missiles. On paper, China has built one of [music] the most sophisticated missile defense networks on the earth. A veritable golden dome to make the rest of the world, America in particular, particularly envious. But paper versus reality, they're two [music] different things. Let's see how it holds up when the missiles actually fly, starting with scenario one.

segments.titre: Scenario one: two Ohio-class submarines fire a limited W88 strike
segments.resume: In the limited scenario two American Ohio-class submarines on hard alert, each with 20 Trident II missiles carrying six warheads, fire 15 to 20 W88 warheads at Chinese targets around Taiwan: the Central Military Commission bunker, DF-41 silos, the Yalong Bay naval base with Jin-class submarines and storage sites. Each W88 is 475 kilotons, about 30 times Hiroshima, with a 25-minute flight, and Chinese satellites spot the rocket plumes immediately.
segments.texte: And this is the version of nuclear war that every one hopes stops here, because the other version doesn't just change the war, it ends the country. Somewhere in the Pacific, two American Ohio-class submarines are on hard alert, which means that they're within range and ready [music] to launch at a moment's notice. Each carries 20 Trident II missiles. Each missile carries six warheads. That is 240 potential nuclear strikes from two boats that nobody can even see coming. Fortunately, their orders are not to usher in an all-out apocalypse, but they know that by sending the message their superiors want delivered, they may very well be the ones to topple the first domino. The target package is 15 to 20 warheads aimed at crippling China's ability to fight back around Taiwan, rather than destroying Chinese civilization entirely. And that's a pretty important distinction. The target list is a greatest hits of things China doesn't really want blown up. The Central Military Commission command bunker outside Beijing, where all the nuclear launch decisions get made. Then there's the DF-41 missile fields scattered along Gansu and Heilongjiang provinces, [music] which are the silos housing China's land-based ICBMs. And then, the Yalong Po naval base on Hainan Island, which just so happens to be home port for many of China's Jin class ballistic missile submarines, each one packing a dozen nuclear missiles of its own. Add in some warhead storage sites in the remote interior, and those early warning radars, and you've got yourself a target package designed to China's ability to fight back. The warheads the Americans would use are W88s, 475 kilotons each, or thereabouts. For reference, the bomb that turned Hiroshima into an ash field was 16 kilotons. These are 30 times more powerful. Flight time from launch to impact is only 25 minutes. The moment those American Trident missiles break the ocean surface, Chinese satellites orbiting the Earth spot the infrared signatures of the rocket motors. It is unavoidable, really. The missile launch is like lighting 20 enormous flares in complete darkness. Alerts start cascading through military networks immediately, and China reacts.

segments.titre: The decision window: Base 37, launch on warning or wait
segments.resume: At Base 37, China's space domain awareness facility, operators need about 60 seconds to confirm the tracks are real. Chinese leaders must decide whether to launch on warning, risking full nuclear war over a contained strike, or wait and risk losing command centers, while limited interceptors force choices about what to defend.
segments.texte: This is the most dangerous phase of any nuclear exchange, the decision window, and it starts with a handful of people staring at a screen. Inside base 37, which is China's space domain [music] awareness facility, operators watch as tracks appear on their monitors. It takes them about 60 seconds [music] to confirm that these are not drills or glitches. These threats are real and they're coming in hot. Chinese leadership now has to make decisions that shape whether this remains limited or spirals out of control. Do they launch on warning, risking full nuclear war if the strike really is contained? Or do they wait, risking the loss of command centers and communications? At the same time, commanders must choose what to defend. Interceptors are limited. Beijing missile silos, submarine [music] bases, not everything can be protected. Every interceptor fired at one target leaves another exposed.

segments.titre: Counterforce strike and civil defense in Chinese megacities
segments.resume: Type 610A radars lock onto the warheads and computers calculate trajectories, revealing the targets as command infrastructure, a counterforce strike aimed at decapitating military capability. Shelters in Chinese megacities are outdated or too far away and mass evacuation is impossible, so civil defense mainly prevents panic.
segments.texte: As the missiles climb above the atmosphere, the ground-based type 610A radars lock onto them. Computer systems start to crunch trajectories, calculating where each warhead is heading. The targets become clear pretty quickly. They're not cities, but command infrastructure. This is what strategists call a counterforce strike aimed at decapitating military capabilities. Civil defense systems act but modern Chinese megacities leave little [music] room for meaningful protection. Shelters exist, but many are outdated, inaccessible, or simply too far away. Evacuating millions of people in such a short space of time is impossible. For most civilians near military targets, [music] survival comes down to where they already are when the warning arrives. At this stage, civil [music] defense is less about saving lives and more about preventing panic.

segments.titre: HQ-29 launch authorizations and the electromagnetic pulse effect
segments.resume: With about 20 minutes left, launch authorizations go to HQ-29 batteries around Beijing and Inner Mongolia with computed firing solutions. Even successful interceptions leave damage beyond the blast radius: bases may lose power, communications and fuel, and electromagnetic pulses fry aircraft avionics so forces survive but coordination unravels.
segments.texte: And by the time China figures it out, there's only about 20 minutes left to respond. Launch authorizations flash to HQ-29 mobile batteries positioned around Beijing and in Inner Mongolia. Commanders receive firing solutions, incredibly complex mathematical calculations that tell each interceptor exactly where to go and when to get there. Even if interceptors succeed, the damage doesn't stop at the blast radius. Bases that survive may still lose power, communication, or fuel storage. [music] Aircraft remain intact, but they can't fly as electromagnetic pulses fry avionics. Units are still alive, but they're cut off. On paper, China still has forces, but in reality, coordination begins to unravel.

segments.titre: Interception math: 40 HQ-29s against 20 warheads
segments.resume: The HQ-29 must physically collide with a warhead moving at 23 times the speed of sound in space and is built to survive extreme G-forces, with two-stage rocket and radar plus infrared guidance. Beijing fires 40 interceptors, two per target, and at an optimistic 85% rate about 16 or 17 intercepts succeed, so three to four warheads get through, roughly 1,425 to 1,900 kilotons or 100 times Hiroshima.
